strings.name: Daron Acemoglu
strings.role: Economist · Institutions, development and technology researcher
strings.summary: Daron Acemoglu studies how political institutions, economic development and technological change shape prosperity and inequality. With collaborators, he combines historical comparison and economic models to examine institutions and their long-run effects and studies automation’s impact on employment. He co-authored Why Nations Fail with James Robinson and explored the distribution of technological gains with Simon Johnson. The three shared the 2024 economics prize for research on institutions and prosperity.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 13 November 2026; selected events reach the formal November 2025 center launch, with status also checked against his 2026 CV. Arguments about institutions and technology are research findings and policy positions, not a single explanation for every country.
strings.influence.rationale: Studied institutions, technology and economic growth, exploring the causes of national prosperity and labor-market change.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: BA, University of York (1989); MSc (1990) and PhD (1992), London School of Economics
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Research on institutions and prosperity
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: Shared the 2024 economics prize with Johnson and Robinson for studies of how institutions form and affect prosperity.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Technology and labor markets
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Studied automation, skills and wages and, with collaborators, examined how technological progress can produce broader gains.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: New research center formally launches
strings.timeline.event-01.text: MIT’s Stone Center, co-directed with David Autor and Simon Johnson, launched to study inequality and the future of work.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Shares the economics prize
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Received the prize with Simon Johnson and James Robinson for research on institutional formation and prosperity.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Co-authors Power and Progress
strings.timeline.event-03.text: With Johnson, examined technological history and argued that the distribution of its gains depends on social and institutional choices.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Named an MIT Institute Professor
strings.timeline.event-04.text: Received MIT’s highest faculty title while continuing research in political economy, development and labor economics.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Co-authors Why Nations Fail
strings.timeline.event-05.text: With Robinson, explained institutional arguments about differences in national development to a wide readership.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Receives the John Bates Clark Medal
strings.timeline.event-06.text: The American Economic Association recognized his contributions to economic research.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Joins MIT
strings.timeline.event-07.text: After lecturing at the London School of Economics, became an MIT assistant professor and established a long-term academic base.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Earns an LSE doctorate
strings.timeline.event-08.text: Completed doctoral work on the microfoundations of macroeconomics, contracts and economic performance.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Completes a master’s degree
strings.timeline.event-09.text: Earned an MSc at the London School of Economics, continuing training in economic theory and empirical research.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Graduates from York
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Completed undergraduate studies at the University of York before graduate work at the London School of Economics.
strings.timeline.event-11.title: Born in Istanbul
strings.timeline.event-11.text: Born in Istanbul, Türkiye, and later studied in Britain before teaching in the United States.
